activities.contextMeaning: Drawing and making things were normal at Tove’s home
activities.sentence: Tove Jansson was born in Helsinki, Finland, in 1914, and she died in 2001. Her life covered almost the whole twentieth century, with all its wars and changes. She grew up in an artistic family. Her mother was an illustrator and her father was a sculptor, so drawing and making things were normal, everyday activities in her home. Tove was a Swedish-speaking Finn. This is important: Finland has two national languages, Finnish and Swedish, and Tove belonged to the smaller Swedish-speaking minority. She wrote all of her books in Swedish, not in Finnish. In a way, she was already a kind of outsider in her own country, and this feeling appears again and again in her stories. Before she became famous as an author, Tove was a serious painter and illustrator. She studied art in Helsinki, Stockholm, and Paris, and she painted for her whole life. She often said that painting was her real work. She also drew political cartoons during the Second World War for a magazine called Garm, where she made fun of dictators like Hitler and Stalin. So when she started writing about small, round creatures in a peaceful valley, she was not a naive young woman. She was an adult artist who had seen war, fear, and hate, and who wanted to imagine a kinder world.

age.contextMeaning: Different ages of people in stories who love and care for each other
age.sentence: The Moomins did not stay only in books. From 1954, Tove Jansson drew a Moomin comic strip for The Evening News, a big newspaper in London. The strip appeared every day and reached millions of readers around the world. This was hard work, and later her brother Lars took over most of the drawing. Because of this comic strip, the Moomins became truly international, known far outside the Nordic countries. Tove Jansson also wrote for adults. In 1972, she published The Summer Book, a quiet novel about an old woman and her small granddaughter spending summers together on a tiny island. There are no Moomins in it, but the same feeling is there: small moments, honest feelings, and love between people who are very different in age. The Moomins arrived in Japan in a very big way in 1990, when the anime Tanoshii Moomin Ikka was shown on television. This series was beautiful, calm, and faithful to Jansson's world, and it became extremely popular. For many Japanese fans, this anime is their first and deepest memory of the Moomins. In 2019, Moominvalley Park opened in Hanno, in Saitama prefecture, near Tokyo. It is the only Moomin theme park in the world outside Finland, and many Japanese learners of English have already visited it. Standing in that park, next to a wooden Moomin House by a lake, you can feel how far a small Swedish-language book from 1945 has traveled.

allowed.contextMeaning: People who feel different are given a chance to belong
allowed.sentence: Tove Jansson, born in Helsinki in 1914 and died in 2001, was a Swedish-speaking Finn who worked first as a painter and illustrator and then as a writer. Just after the Second World War, she began the Moomin stories with The Moomins and the Great Flood in 1945, followed by Comet in Moominland in 1946 and Finn Family Moomintroll in 1948. She created a family — Moomintroll, Moominmamma, Moominpappa — and a circle of outsiders like the free spirit Snufkin and the fierce Little My. From 1954, her Moomin comic strip in London's The Evening News brought the characters to millions of readers. In 1972 she wrote The Summer Book for adults, and in 1990 the anime Tanoshii Moomin Ikka made the Moomins deeply loved in Japan, where Moominvalley Park later opened in Hanno, Saitama in 2019. Under all the cute pictures, the message is simple and serious: the world needs quiet places where people who feel different are welcome, listened to, and allowed to belong.

She created a family — Moomintroll, Moominmamma, Moominpappa — and a circle of outsiders like the free spirit Snufkin and the fierce Little My. From 1954, her Moomin comic strip in London's The Evening News brought the characters to millions of readers. In 1972 she wrote The Summer Book for adults, and in 1990 the anime Tanoshii Moomin Ikka made the Moomins deeply loved in Japan, where Moominvalley Park later opened in Hanno, Saitama in 2019. Under all the cute pictures, the message is simple and serious: the world needs quiet places where people who feel different are welcome, listened to, and allowed to belong.

appeared.contextMeaning: The Moomin comic was shown every day in a big newspaper
appeared.sentence: The Moomins did not stay only in books. From 1954, Tove Jansson drew a Moomin comic strip for The Evening News, a big newspaper in London. The strip appeared every day and reached millions of readers around the world. This was hard work, and later her brother Lars took over most of the drawing. Because of this comic strip, the Moomins became truly international, known far outside the Nordic countries. Tove Jansson also wrote for adults. In 1972, she published The Summer Book, a quiet novel about an old woman and her small granddaughter spending summers together on a tiny island. There are no Moomins in it, but the same feeling is there: small moments, honest feelings, and love between people who are very different in age. The Moomins arrived in Japan in a very big way in 1990, when the anime Tanoshii Moomin Ikka was shown on television. This series was beautiful, calm, and faithful to Jansson's world, and it became extremely popular. For many Japanese fans, this anime is their first and deepest memory of the Moomins. In 2019, Moominvalley Park opened in Hanno, in Saitama prefecture, near Tokyo. It is the only Moomin theme park in the world outside Finland, and many Japanese learners of English have already visited it. Standing in that park, next to a wooden Moomin House by a lake, you can feel how far a small Swedish-language book from 1945 has traveled.

appears.contextMeaning: The feeling of being an outsider comes again and again in stories
appears.sentence: Tove Jansson was born in Helsinki, Finland, in 1914, and she died in 2001. Her life covered almost the whole twentieth century, with all its wars and changes. She grew up in an artistic family. Her mother was an illustrator and her father was a sculptor, so drawing and making things were normal, everyday activities in her home. Tove was a Swedish-speaking Finn. This is important: Finland has two national languages, Finnish and Swedish, and Tove belonged to the smaller Swedish-speaking minority. She wrote all of her books in Swedish, not in Finnish. In a way, she was already a kind of outsider in her own country, and this feeling appears again and again in her stories. Before she became famous as an author, Tove was a serious painter and illustrator. She studied art in Helsinki, Stockholm, and Paris, and she painted for her whole life. She often said that painting was her real work. She also drew political cartoons during the Second World War for a magazine called Garm, where she made fun of dictators like Hitler and Stalin. So when she started writing about small, round creatures in a peaceful valley, she was not a naive young woman. She was an adult artist who had seen war, fear, and hate, and who wanted to imagine a kinder world.

art.sentence: Tove Jansson was born in Helsinki, Finland, in 1914, and she died in 2001. Her life covered almost the whole twentieth century, with all its wars and changes. She grew up in an artistic family. Her mother was an illustrator and her father was a sculptor, so drawing and making things were normal, everyday activities in her home. Tove was a Swedish-speaking Finn. This is important: Finland has two national languages, Finnish and Swedish, and Tove belonged to the smaller Swedish-speaking minority. She wrote all of her books in Swedish, not in Finnish. In a way, she was already a kind of outsider in her own country, and this feeling appears again and again in her stories. Before she became famous as an author, Tove was a serious painter and illustrator. She studied art in Helsinki, Stockholm, and Paris, and she painted for her whole life. She often said that painting was her real work. She also drew political cartoons during the Second World War for a magazine called Garm, where she made fun of dictators like Hitler and Stalin. So when she started writing about small, round creatures in a peaceful valley, she was not a naive young woman. She was an adult artist who had seen war, fear, and hate, and who wanted to imagine a kinder world.

ask.simpleMeaning: To say questions to learn or know
ask.contextMeaning: Moomintroll asks important questions that many children wonder about
ask.sentence: The Moomin stories are famous for their characters, and almost all of them are, in some way, outsiders. At the center is Moomintroll, a young Moomin who is curious, sensitive, and sometimes afraid. He asks the questions that many children and shy adults are afraid to ask: Am I loved? Will my friend come back? What happens if everything changes? His mother, Moominmamma, is calm and warm. She carries a handbag full of useful things and she always has time to listen. For many readers, she is one of the kindest mothers in all of children's literature. Moominpappa is more dramatic. He wears a tall black hat, writes his memoirs, and dreams of adventures on the sea. He can be silly, but he loves his family. Around this family come the visitors. Snufkin is a quiet, free spirit who travels alone with a green hat and a small tent. He leaves every autumn and returns every spring, and Moomintroll waits for him like we wait for a best friend. Little My is small, sharp, and fierce. She says exactly what she thinks and is never polite just to be nice. There are also stranger creatures: the lonely Groke, who freezes the ground where she sits because no one has ever loved her, and the shy Hattifatteners, who travel in silent groups toward the horizon. Together, these characters show a simple, powerful idea: a good community is not one where everyone is the same, but one where very different people are welcome.

Will my friend come back? What happens if everything changes? His mother, Moominmamma, is calm and warm. She carries a handbag full of useful things and she always has time to listen. For many readers, she is one of the kindest mothers in all of children's literature. Moominpappa is more dramatic. He wears a tall black hat, writes his memoirs, and dreams of adventures on the sea. He can be silly, but he loves his family. Around this family come the visitors. Snufkin is a quiet, free spirit who travels alone with a green hat and a small tent. He leaves every autumn and returns every spring, and Moomintroll waits for him like we wait for a best friend. Little My is small, sharp, and fierce. She says exactly what she thinks and is never polite just to be nice. There are also stranger creatures: the lonely Groke, who freezes the ground where she sits because no one has ever loved her, and the shy Hattifatteners, who travel in silent groups toward the horizon. Together, these characters show a simple, powerful idea: a good community is not one where everyone is the same, but one where very different people are welcome.

began.contextMeaning: Tove Jansson started writing Moomin stories after World War II
began.sentence: Tove Jansson, born in Helsinki in 1914 and died in 2001, was a Swedish-speaking Finn who worked first as a painter and illustrator and then as a writer. Just after the Second World War, she began the Moomin stories with The Moomins and the Great Flood in 1945, followed by Comet in Moominland in 1946 and Finn Family Moomintroll in 1948. She created a family — Moomintroll, Moominmamma, Moominpappa — and a circle of outsiders like the free spirit Snufkin and the fierce Little My. From 1954, her Moomin comic strip in London's The Evening News brought the characters to millions of readers. In 1972 she wrote The Summer Book for adults, and in 1990 the anime Tanoshii Moomin Ikka made the Moomins deeply loved in Japan, where Moominvalley Park later opened in Hanno, Saitama in 2019. Under all the cute pictures, the message is simple and serious: the world needs quiet places where people who feel different are welcome, listened to, and allowed to belong.

behind.sentence: The first Moomin book, called The Moomins and the Great Flood, was published in 1945, just after the Second World War ended. This is an important detail. Europe was tired, broken, and full of families who had lost their homes. In this small book, a mother Moomin and her child are searching for the missing father, walking through a strange and frightening world of dark forests and rising water. It is a story about being lost and looking for family — exactly what many real people felt in 1945. The next book, Comet in Moominland, came out in 1946. In this story, a huge comet is coming to destroy the world, and the Moomins must travel to find out if they can survive. Again, the story is gentle, but the fear behind it is real: children in 1946 knew what it was like to hear that the world could end. Then, in 1948, Jansson published Finn Family Moomintroll, which is often the first Moomin book that readers meet today. This one is warmer, funnier, and full of magic hats and small adventures. Together, these three early books built the world of Moominvalley: a place where scary things happen, but where a family and their friends always come home to a lamp in the window and warm soup on the table.

best.contextMeaning: Moomintroll waits for Snufkin like waiting for a favorite friend
best.sentence: The Moomin stories are famous for their characters, and almost all of them are, in some way, outsiders. At the center is Moomintroll, a young Moomin who is curious, sensitive, and sometimes afraid. He asks the questions that many children and shy adults are afraid to ask: Am I loved? Will my friend come back? What happens if everything changes? His mother, Moominmamma, is calm and warm. She carries a handbag full of useful things and she always has time to listen. For many readers, she is one of the kindest mothers in all of children's literature. Moominpappa is more dramatic. He wears a tall black hat, writes his memoirs, and dreams of adventures on the sea. He can be silly, but he loves his family. Around this family come the visitors. Snufkin is a quiet, free spirit who travels alone with a green hat and a small tent. He leaves every autumn and returns every spring, and Moomintroll waits for him like we wait for a best friend. Little My is small, sharp, and fierce. She says exactly what she thinks and is never polite just to be nice. There are also stranger creatures: the lonely Groke, who freezes the ground where she sits because no one has ever loved her, and the shy Hattifatteners, who travel in silent groups toward the horizon. Together, these characters show a simple, powerful idea: a good community is not one where everyone is the same, but one where very different people are welcome.

brother.simpleMeaning: A boy or man with the same parents as you
brother.contextMeaning: Tove Jansson's brother Lars helped draw the Moomin comic strip
brother.sentence: The Moomins did not stay only in books. From 1954, Tove Jansson drew a Moomin comic strip for The Evening News, a big newspaper in London. The strip appeared every day and reached millions of readers around the world. This was hard work, and later her brother Lars took over most of the drawing. Because of this comic strip, the Moomins became truly international, known far outside the Nordic countries. Tove Jansson also wrote for adults. In 1972, she published The Summer Book, a quiet novel about an old woman and her small granddaughter spending summers together on a tiny island. There are no Moomins in it, but the same feeling is there: small moments, honest feelings, and love between people who are very different in age. The Moomins arrived in Japan in a very big way in 1990, when the anime Tanoshii Moomin Ikka was shown on television. This series was beautiful, calm, and faithful to Jansson's world, and it became extremely popular. For many Japanese fans, this anime is their first and deepest memory of the Moomins. In 2019, Moominvalley Park opened in Hanno, in Saitama prefecture, near Tokyo. It is the only Moomin theme park in the world outside Finland, and many Japanese learners of English have already visited it. Standing in that park, next to a wooden Moomin House by a lake, you can feel how far a small Swedish-language book from 1945 has traveled.

The strip appeared every day and reached millions of readers around the world. This was hard work, and later her brother Lars took over most of the drawing. Because of this comic strip, the Moomins became truly international, known far outside the Nordic countries. Tove Jansson also wrote for adults. In 1972, she published The Summer Book, a quiet novel about an old woman and her small granddaughter spending summers together on a tiny island. There are no Moomins in it, but the same feeling is there: small moments, honest feelings, and love between people who are very different in age. The Moomins arrived in Japan in a very big way in 1990, when the anime Tanoshii Moomin Ikka was shown on television. This series was beautiful, calm, and faithful to Jansson's world, and it became extremely popular. For many Japanese fans, this anime is their first and deepest memory of the Moomins. In 2019, Moominvalley Park opened in Hanno, in Saitama prefecture, near Tokyo. It is the only Moomin theme park in the world outside Finland, and many Japanese learners of English have already visited it. Standing in that park, next to a wooden Moomin House by a lake, you can feel how far a small Swedish-language book from 1945 has traveled.

brought.sentence: Tove Jansson, born in Helsinki in 1914 and died in 2001, was a Swedish-speaking Finn who worked first as a painter and illustrator and then as a writer. Just after the Second World War, she began the Moomin stories with The Moomins and the Great Flood in 1945, followed by Comet in Moominland in 1946 and Finn Family Moomintroll in 1948. She created a family — Moomintroll, Moominmamma, Moominpappa — and a circle of outsiders like the free spirit Snufkin and the fierce Little My. From 1954, her Moomin comic strip in London's The Evening News brought the characters to millions of readers. In 1972 she wrote The Summer Book for adults, and in 1990 the anime Tanoshii Moomin Ikka made the Moomins deeply loved in Japan, where Moominvalley Park later opened in Hanno, Saitama in 2019. Under all the cute pictures, the message is simple and serious: the world needs quiet places where people who feel different are welcome, listened to, and allowed to belong.

built.contextMeaning: The early books made the world of Moominvalley
built.sentence: The first Moomin book, called The Moomins and the Great Flood, was published in 1945, just after the Second World War ended. This is an important detail. Europe was tired, broken, and full of families who had lost their homes. In this small book, a mother Moomin and her child are searching for the missing father, walking through a strange and frightening world of dark forests and rising water. It is a story about being lost and looking for family — exactly what many real people felt in 1945. The next book, Comet in Moominland, came out in 1946. In this story, a huge comet is coming to destroy the world, and the Moomins must travel to find out if they can survive. Again, the story is gentle, but the fear behind it is real: children in 1946 knew what it was like to hear that the world could end. Then, in 1948, Jansson published Finn Family Moomintroll, which is often the first Moomin book that readers meet today. This one is warmer, funnier, and full of magic hats and small adventures. Together, these three early books built the world of Moominvalley: a place where scary things happen, but where a family and their friends always come home to a lamp in the window and warm soup on the table.

center.simpleMeaning: The middle or most important part
center.contextMeaning: Moomintroll is the main character in the stories
center.sentence: The Moomin stories are famous for their characters, and almost all of them are, in some way, outsiders. At the center is Moomintroll, a young Moomin who is curious, sensitive, and sometimes afraid. He asks the questions that many children and shy adults are afraid to ask: Am I loved? Will my friend come back? What happens if everything changes? His mother, Moominmamma, is calm and warm. She carries a handbag full of useful things and she always has time to listen. For many readers, she is one of the kindest mothers in all of children's literature. Moominpappa is more dramatic. He wears a tall black hat, writes his memoirs, and dreams of adventures on the sea. He can be silly, but he loves his family. Around this family come the visitors. Snufkin is a quiet, free spirit who travels alone with a green hat and a small tent. He leaves every autumn and returns every spring, and Moomintroll waits for him like we wait for a best friend. Little My is small, sharp, and fierce. She says exactly what she thinks and is never polite just to be nice. There are also stranger creatures: the lonely Groke, who freezes the ground where she sits because no one has ever loved her, and the shy Hattifatteners, who travel in silent groups toward the horizon. Together, these characters show a simple, powerful idea: a good community is not one where everyone is the same, but one where very different people are welcome.

century.sentence: Tove Jansson was born in Helsinki, Finland, in 1914, and she died in 2001. Her life covered almost the whole twentieth century, with all its wars and changes. She grew up in an artistic family. Her mother was an illustrator and her father was a sculptor, so drawing and making things were normal, everyday activities in her home. Tove was a Swedish-speaking Finn. This is important: Finland has two national languages, Finnish and Swedish, and Tove belonged to the smaller Swedish-speaking minority. She wrote all of her books in Swedish, not in Finnish. In a way, she was already a kind of outsider in her own country, and this feeling appears again and again in her stories. Before she became famous as an author, Tove was a serious painter and illustrator. She studied art in Helsinki, Stockholm, and Paris, and she painted for her whole life. countries.sentence: The Moomins did not stay only in books. From 1954, Tove Jansson drew a Moomin comic strip for The Evening News, a big newspaper in London. The strip appeared every day and reached millions of readers around the world. This was hard work, and later her brother Lars took over most of the drawing. Because of this comic strip, the Moomins became truly international, known far outside the Nordic countries. Tove Jansson also wrote for adults. In 1972, she published The Summer Book, a quiet novel about an old woman and her small granddaughter spending summers together on a tiny island. There are no Moomins in it, but the same feeling is there: small moments, honest feelings, and love between people who are very different in age. The Moomins arrived in Japan in a very big way in 1990, when the anime Tanoshii Moomin Ikka was shown on television. This series was beautiful, calm, and faithful to Jansson's world, and it became extremely popular. For many Japanese fans, this anime is their first and deepest memory of the Moomins. In 2019, Moominvalley Park opened in Hanno, in Saitama prefecture, near Tokyo. It is the only Moomin theme park in the world outside Finland, and many Japanese learners of English have already visited it. Standing in that park, next to a wooden Moomin House by a lake, you can feel how far a small Swedish-language book from 1945 has traveled.

created.sentence: Tove Jansson, born in Helsinki in 1914 and died in 2001, was a Swedish-speaking Finn who worked first as a painter and illustrator and then as a writer. Just after the Second World War, she began the Moomin stories with The Moomins and the Great Flood in 1945, followed by Comet in Moominland in 1946 and Finn Family Moomintroll in 1948. She created a family — Moomintroll, Moominmamma, Moominpappa — and a circle of outsiders like the free spirit Snufkin and the fierce Little My. From 1954, her Moomin comic strip in London's The Evening News brought the characters to millions of readers. In 1972 she wrote The Summer Book for adults, and in 1990 the anime Tanoshii Moomin Ikka made the Moomins deeply loved in Japan, where Moominvalley Park later opened in Hanno, Saitama in 2019. Under all the cute pictures, the message is simple and serious: the world needs quiet places where people who feel different are welcome, listened to, and allowed to belong.

curious.simpleMeaning: Wanting to learn or know about things
curious.contextMeaning: Moomintroll wants to know answers and asks many questions
curious.sentence: The Moomin stories are famous for their characters, and almost all of them are, in some way, outsiders. At the center is Moomintroll, a young Moomin who is curious, sensitive, and sometimes afraid. He asks the questions that many children and shy adults are afraid to ask: Am I loved? Will my friend come back? What happens if everything changes? His mother, Moominmamma, is calm and warm. She carries a handbag full of useful things and she always has time to listen. For many readers, she is one of the kindest mothers in all of children's literature. Moominpappa is more dramatic. He wears a tall black hat, writes his memoirs, and dreams of adventures on the sea. He can be silly, but he loves his family. Around this family come the visitors. Snufkin is a quiet, free spirit who travels alone with a green hat and a small tent. He leaves every autumn and returns every spring, and Moomintroll waits for him like we wait for a best friend. Little My is small, sharp, and fierce. day.contextMeaning: The Moomin comic strip was shown every day in the newspaper
day.sentence: The Moomins did not stay only in books. From 1954, Tove Jansson drew a Moomin comic strip for The Evening News, a big newspaper in London. The strip appeared every day and reached millions of readers around the world. This was hard work, and later her brother Lars took over most of the drawing. Because of this comic strip, the Moomins became truly international, known far outside the Nordic countries. Tove Jansson also wrote for adults. In 1972, she published The Summer Book, a quiet novel about an old woman and her small granddaughter spending summers together on a tiny island. There are no Moomins in it, but the same feeling is there: small moments, honest feelings, and love between people who are very different in age. The Moomins arrived in Japan in a very big way in 1990, when the anime Tanoshii Moomin Ikka was shown on television. This series was beautiful, calm, and faithful to Jansson's world, and it became extremely popular. For many Japanese fans, this anime is their first and deepest memory of the Moomins. In 2019, Moominvalley Park opened in Hanno, in Saitama prefecture, near Tokyo. It is the only Moomin theme park in the world outside Finland, and many Japanese learners of English have already visited it. Standing in that park, next to a wooden Moomin House by a lake, you can feel how far a small Swedish-language book from 1945 has traveled.

deeper.sentence: Some stories look small and sweet on the outside, but they carry a serious idea inside. The Moomin stories by Tove Jansson are like that. On the surface, they are gentle tales about round white creatures who look a little like hippos, living in a green valley in Finland. Underneath, they are about something deeper: making room in the world for people who feel different, strange, lonely, or lost. You will learn about Tove Jansson's life, her books, her famous comic strip, and how the Moomins became so loved in Japan. Your goal is to understand both the fun surface of Moominvalley and the quiet, kind idea that lives under it, and to talk about why this idea still matters today.

deeply.sentence: Tove Jansson, born in Helsinki in 1914 and died in 2001, was a Swedish-speaking Finn who worked first as a painter and illustrator and then as a writer. Just after the Second World War, she began the Moomin stories with The Moomins and the Great Flood in 1945, followed by Comet in Moominland in 1946 and Finn Family Moomintroll in 1948. She created a family — Moomintroll, Moominmamma, Moominpappa — and a circle of outsiders like the free spirit Snufkin and the fierce Little My. From 1954, her Moomin comic strip in London's The Evening News brought the characters to millions of readers. In 1972 she wrote The Summer Book for adults, and in 1990 the anime Tanoshii Moomin Ikka made the Moomins deeply loved in Japan, where Moominvalley Park later opened in Hanno, Saitama in 2019. Under all the cute pictures, the message is simple and serious: the world needs quiet places where people who feel different are welcome, listened to, and allowed to belong.

detail.simpleMeaning: A small fact or piece of information
detail.contextMeaning: The time when the first Moomin book was published is important
detail.sentence: The first Moomin book, called The Moomins and the Great Flood, was published in 1945, just after the Second World War ended. This is an important detail. Europe was tired, broken, and full of families who had lost their homes. In this small book, a mother Moomin and her child are searching for the missing father, walking through a strange and frightening world of dark forests and rising water. It is a story about being lost and looking for family — exactly what many real people felt in 1945. The next book, Comet in Moominland, came out in 1946. In this story, a huge comet is coming to destroy the world, and the Moomins must travel to find out if they can survive. Again, the story is gentle, but the fear behind it is real: children in 1946 knew what it was like to hear that the world could end. Then, in 1948, Jansson published Finn Family Moomintroll, which is often the first Moomin book that readers meet today. This one is warmer, funnier, and full of magic hats and small adventures. Together, these three early books built the world of Moominvalley: a place where scary things happen, but where a family and their friends always come home to a lamp in the window and warm soup on the table.

dramatic.sentence: The Moomin stories are famous for their characters, and almost all of them are, in some way, outsiders. At the center is Moomintroll, a young Moomin who is curious, sensitive, and sometimes afraid. He asks the questions that many children and shy adults are afraid to ask: Am I loved? Will my friend come back? What happens if everything changes? His mother, Moominmamma, is calm and warm. She carries a handbag full of useful things and she always has time to listen. For many readers, she is one of the kindest mothers in all of children's literature. Moominpappa is more dramatic. He wears a tall black hat, writes his memoirs, and dreams of adventures on the sea. He can be silly, but he loves his family. Around this family come the visitors. Snufkin is a quiet, free spirit who travels alone with a green hat and a small tent. He leaves every autumn and returns every spring, and Moomintroll waits for him like we wait for a best friend. Little My is small, sharp, and fierce. She says exactly what she thinks and is never polite just to be nice. There are also stranger creatures: the lonely Groke, who freezes the ground where she sits because no one has ever loved her, and the shy Hattifatteners, who travel in silent groups toward the horizon. Together, these characters show a simple, powerful idea: a good community is not one where everyone is the same, but one where very different people are welcome.

english.sentence: The Moomins did not stay only in books. From 1954, Tove Jansson drew a Moomin comic strip for The Evening News, a big newspaper in London. The strip appeared every day and reached millions of readers around the world. This was hard work, and later her brother Lars took over most of the drawing. Because of this comic strip, the Moomins became truly international, known far outside the Nordic countries. Tove Jansson also wrote for adults. In 1972, she published The Summer Book, a quiet novel about an old woman and her small granddaughter spending summers together on a tiny island. There are no Moomins in it, but the same feeling is there: small moments, honest feelings, and love between people who are very different in age. The Moomins arrived in Japan in a very big way in 1990, when the anime Tanoshii Moomin Ikka was shown on television. This series was beautiful, calm, and faithful to Jansson's world, and it became extremely popular. For many Japanese fans, this anime is their first and deepest memory of the Moomins. In 2019, Moominvalley Park opened in Hanno, in Saitama prefecture, near Tokyo. It is the only Moomin theme park in the world outside Finland, and many Japanese learners of English have already visited it. Standing in that park, next to a wooden Moomin House by a lake, you can feel how far a small Swedish-language book from 1945 has traveled.

europe.simpleMeaning: A big group of countries on one big land
europe.contextMeaning: The place tired and broken after the Second World War ended
europe.sentence: The first Moomin book, called The Moomins and the Great Flood, was published in 1945, just after the Second World War ended. This is an important detail. Europe was tired, broken, and full of families who had lost their homes. In this small book, a mother Moomin and her child are searching for the missing father, walking through a strange and frightening world of dark forests and rising water. It is a story about being lost and looking for family — exactly what many real people felt in 1945. The next book, Comet in Moominland, came out in 1946. In this story, a huge comet is coming to destroy the world, and the Moomins must travel to find out if they can survive. Again, the story is gentle, but the fear behind it is real: children in 1946 knew what it was like to hear that the world could end. Then, in 1948, Jansson published Finn Family Moomintroll, which is often the first Moomin book that readers meet today. This one is warmer, funnier, and full of magic hats and small adventures. Together, these three early books built the world of Moominvalley: a place where scary things happen, but where a family and their friends always come home to a lamp in the window and warm soup on the table.

everyday.contextMeaning: Normal things done often in Tove Jansson’s home
everyday.sentence: Tove Jansson was born in Helsinki, Finland, in 1914, and she died in 2001. Her life covered almost the whole twentieth century, with all its wars and changes. She grew up in an artistic family. Her mother was an illustrator and her father was a sculptor, so drawing and making things were normal, everyday activities in her home. Tove was a Swedish-speaking Finn. This is important: Finland has two national languages, Finnish and Swedish, and Tove belonged to the smaller Swedish-speaking minority. She wrote all of her books in Swedish, not in Finnish. In a way, she was already a kind of outsider in her own country, and this feeling appears again and again in her stories. Before she became famous as an author, Tove was a serious painter and illustrator. She studied art in Helsinki, Stockholm, and Paris, and she painted for her whole life. She often said that painting was her real work. She also drew political cartoons during the Second World War for a magazine called Garm, where she made fun of dictators like Hitler and Stalin. So when she started writing about small, round creatures in a peaceful valley, she was not a naive young woman. She was an adult artist who had seen war, fear, and hate, and who wanted to imagine a kinder world.

everyone.simpleMeaning: All the people, no one left out
everyone.contextMeaning: All different people are welcome in a good community
everyone.sentence: The Moomin stories are famous for their characters, and almost all of them are, in some way, outsiders. At the center is Moomintroll, a young Moomin who is curious, sensitive, and sometimes afraid. He asks the questions that many children and shy adults are afraid to ask: Am I loved? Will my friend come back? What happens if everything changes? His mother, Moominmamma, is calm and warm. She carries a handbag full of useful things and she always has time to listen. For many readers, she is one of the kindest mothers in all of children's literature. Moominpappa is more dramatic. He wears a tall black hat, writes his memoirs, and dreams of adventures on the sea. He can be silly, but he loves his family. Around this family come the visitors. Snufkin is a quiet, free spirit who travels alone with a green hat and a small tent. He leaves every autumn and returns every spring, and Moomintroll waits for him like we wait for a best friend. Little My is small, sharp, and fierce. She says exactly what she thinks and is never polite just to be nice. There are also stranger creatures: the lonely Groke, who freezes the ground where she sits because no one has ever loved her, and the shy Hattifatteners, who travel in silent groups toward the horizon. Together, these characters show a simple, powerful idea: a good community is not one where everyone is the same, but one where very different people are welcome.

Will my friend come back? What happens if everything changes? His mother, Moominmamma, is calm and warm. She carries a handbag full of useful things and she always has time to listen. For many readers, she is one of the kindest mothers in all of children's literature. Moominpappa is more dramatic. He wears a tall black hat, writes his memoirs, and dreams of adventures on the sea. He can be silly, but he loves his family. Around this family come the visitors. Snufkin is a quiet, free spirit who travels alone with a green hat and a small tent. He leaves every autumn and returns every spring, and Moomintroll waits for him like we wait for a best friend. Little My is small, sharp, and fierce. She says exactly what she thinks and is never polite just to be nice. There are also stranger creatures: the lonely Groke, who freezes the ground where she sits because no one has ever loved her, and the shy Hattifatteners, who travel in silent groups toward the horizon. Together, these characters show a simple, powerful idea: a good community is not one where everyone is the same, but one where very different people are welcome.

extremely.sentence: The Moomins did not stay only in books. From 1954, Tove Jansson drew a Moomin comic strip for The Evening News, a big newspaper in London. The strip appeared every day and reached millions of readers around the world. This was hard work, and later her brother Lars took over most of the drawing. Because of this comic strip, the Moomins became truly international, known far outside the Nordic countries. Tove Jansson also wrote for adults. In 1972, she published The Summer Book, a quiet novel about an old woman and her small granddaughter spending summers together on a tiny island. There are no Moomins in it, but the same feeling is there: small moments, honest feelings, and love between people who are very different in age. The Moomins arrived in Japan in a very big way in 1990, when the anime Tanoshii Moomin Ikka was shown on television. This series was beautiful, calm, and faithful to Jansson's world, and it became extremely popular. For many Japanese fans, this anime is their first and deepest memory of the Moomins. In 2019, Moominvalley Park opened in Hanno, in Saitama prefecture, near Tokyo. It is the only Moomin theme park in the world outside Finland, and many Japanese learners of English have already visited it. Standing in that park, next to a wooden Moomin House by a lake, you can feel how far a small Swedish-language book from 1945 has traveled.
